questions.explanation: Locsin's most philosophically significant concept — the 'floating volume' — is a Modernist reinterpretation of the bahay kubo's raised floor. The bahay kubo elevates its living space above flood level, creating a ventilated silong (open space under the floor). Locsin takes this spatial concept — a raised volume over a void — and executes it in Brutalist concrete. The Tanghalang Pambansa appears to hover above its reflecting pool. Critically, this is an ABSTRACT reinterpretation, not a material one: Locsin uses raw concrete (béton brut), not bamboo and nipa. This places him in the First Wave (Modernist/Brutalist) rather than the Second Wave (Neo-Vernacular) — Locsin expresses Filipino identity through spatial concepts, Mañosa through materials.

questions.explanation: The Coconut Palace (Tahanang Pilipino), completed in 1980 in the CCP Complex, is Mañosa's most iconic Neo-Vernacular building. It is clad in coconut lumber (coco lumber) throughout — posts, beams, floors, and panels — alongside other indigenous materials. The building embodies Mañosa's FCC framework: Filipino values (ornate Philippine cultural motifs), Climate response (high ceilings, large windows, low eaves, free indoor-outdoor interchange), Craft/indigenous materials (coconut wood throughout). Critically, the Coconut Palace must not be confused with the Tanghalang Pambansa — same CCP Complex, different architects: Mañosa (Coconut Palace, Neo-Vernatural) vs Locsin (Tanghalang Pambansa, Brutalist Modernism).

questions.explanation: The EDSA Shrine (1989) is one of Mañosa's most significant ecclesiastical works. It embodies his Neo-Vernacular FCC philosophy: (1) FILIPINO VALUES — the shrine commemorates the 1986 People Power Revolution, expressing national identity and spiritual values; (2) CLIMATE RESPONSE — high ceilings, large windows, low eaves, and natural ventilation create a naturally comfortable worship space; (3) CRAFT / INDIGENOUS MATERIALS — bamboo and coconut wood structural and decorative elements, capiz shell panels. The EDSA Shrine is often compared to the Church of the Holy Sacrifice (UP Diliman, by Locsin) — both are iconic Philippine churches, but different architects and styles: Locsin's Brutalist Modernism vs Mañosa's Neo-Vernacular.

questions.explanation: Francisco Mañosa's FCC framework is his philosophical test for whether a building is genuinely Filipino: (1) FILIPINO VALUES — architecture must reflect Filipino cultural values: family and community (expressed through spatial openness, transitional indoor-outdoor spaces), the tradition of ornamentation, and bayanihan; (2) CLIMATE RESPONSE — the building must respond to the tropical Philippine climate through passive strategies: overhangs, cross-ventilation, elevated floors, high ceilings; (3) CRAFT / INDIGENOUS MATERIALS — the building must use Filipino indigenous materials: bamboo (kawayan), coconut wood (coco lumber), rattan, capiz shells, volcanic rock (adobe), anahaw palm (thatch), clay tiles (teja).

questions.explanation: The three waves of Filipino identity architecture: (1) FIRST WAVE (Modernist/Brutalist, 1950s–1970s): Key figures = Leandro Locsin, Cesar Concio, Gabriel Formoso, Felipe Mendoza. Landmark buildings = CCP Complex (Tanghalang Pambansa), PICC, UP Holy Sacrifice Church. (2) SECOND WAVE (Neo-Vernacular, 1970s–2000s): Key figure = Francisco Mañosa. Buildings = Coconut Palace, San Miguel HQ, EDSA Shrine, Amanpulo Resort. (3) THIRD WAVE (Contemporary Tropical, 2000s–present): Key firms = BUDJI+ROYAL, WTA Architecture.

questions.explanation: Leandro Locsin (1928–1994, National Artist 1990) belongs to the First Wave of Filipino architecture (Modernist/Brutalist, 1950s–1970s). His signature concept is the 'floating volume' — the appearance of massive concrete forms levitating above the ground, seen most dramatically in the Tanghalang Pambansa (CCP Main Theater). The optical illusion is created by recessing the structural base and cantilevering the upper mass. Critically, this concept is inspired by the bahay kubo's raised floor — the under-floor ventilation space is reinterpreted as a visual void beneath a hovering concrete volume. Locsin's buildings are Brutalist concrete, not Neo-Vernacular. Mañosa is the Neo-Vernacular architect.

questions.explanation: The Third Wave of Filipino architecture (2000s–present) includes firms like BUDJI+ROYAL, WTA Architecture + Design, and Mañosa & Company (continuing under Gelo Mañosa). BUDJI+ROYAL is notable for: (1) Integrating BERDE (Philippine Green Building Rating System) and LEED (international) certification requirements with Filipino spatial traditions; (2) Using bamboo engineering — engineered bamboo as structural elements, not just decorative; (3) Earth-mass design — using the thermal mass of earth/adobe/stone to regulate interior temperature; (4) Computational tools — parametric design and digital fabrication alongside traditional craft.
